name: רְעוּאֵל
gloss: friend of God; or God shepherds
summary: Borne by four men: the priest of Midian, father of Zipporah and of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, called Jethro elsewhere (Exo 2:16–21; 3:1; Num 10:29); a son of Esau by Basemath, father of Edomite chiefs (Gen 36:4, 10–17); a Benjamite of the return (1Ch 9:8); and the Gadite whom Num 2:14 so names, Deuel elsewhere. The name joins אֵל “God” to the root’s letters with the linking -וּ- of פְּנוּאֵל “face of God”, which the text itself explains (Gen 32:31). Read with רֵעַ “friend”, as Yahweh spoke with Moses “as a man speaks to his רֵעַ” (Exo 33:11), it is “friend of God”; read with the verb “shepherd”, as Jacob’s “God who shepherded me” (Gen 48:15), “God shepherds”. The form does not settle which.

evidence.note: Zipporah and her sisters “came to רְעוּאֵל their father”, the priest of Midian, after Moses watered their flock.
Moses said “to Hobab the son of רְעוּאֵל the Midianite, Moses’ father-in-law: We are setting out.”
Moses “was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian”: the same man under another name.
“These are the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, chief Mizzah.”
Among the Benjamites in Jerusalem: Meshullam son of Shephatiah, son of רְעוּאֵל, son of Ibnijah.
“Eliasaph the son of רְעוּאֵל”, elsewhere son of Deuel (Num 1:14; 10:20).
פְּנִיאֵל “for I have seen God face to face”; the name is written פְּנוּאֵל in the next verse: noun, linking -וּ-, אֵל.
The root’s noun: “as a man speaks to his רֵעַ”.
The root’s verb: “the God who has shepherded me (הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי)”.

note: TIPNR merges Reuel of Exo 2:18 with Jethro (Jethro@Exo.2.18), and Num 10:29 may make either Hobab or Reuel Moses’ חֹתֵן (see names/hobab.json). Num 2:14 is the only רְעוּאֵל for the Gadite, whose record (Deuel@Num.1.14) is also tagged by names/deuel.json; it is listed here because the word sheet shows this entry on Num 2:14’s token under t.dl.aj. The Greek has Ραγουηλ throughout, and Tobit’s Raguel is the same name. The gloss puts “friend of God” first because Hebrew names in -וּאֵל formed with a noun (פְּנוּאֵל) read noun + God; the verbal reading is not excluded.
